en: From the *Abhidhānottara*: Now I shall proclaim the supreme Yoga of the Buddha-Kāpālika,
the reality that is the highest of all yogas and the bestower of all accomplishments.
Conventionally, one should not disclose this secret to just anyone.
The supreme reality, which is to be grasped through meditative cultivation, resides within the heart of the yogi;
it is hidden, secret, and most secret—one should contemplate it from the mouth of the guru.
In cremation grounds, gardens, and delightful places, the practitioner of firm resolve,
through the yoga of the generation stage (utpattikrama), proceeds according to the sequence of the sacred sites (bhūmipīṭha) and so forth;
[he visualizes] that beautiful [deity] arising from the syllable *HŪṂ* in the center of the two lotuses.
Having transformed that very self into the supreme Buddha-Kāpālin—
peaceful, free from disease, pure, devoid of all conceptual constructions,
arisen from the vowels and consonants, beyond duality, and supremely auspicious— [102]
Having two arms and one face, adorned with the six mudrās and emblems,
with a complexion like that of Jambūnada gold, blazing and filled with rays of light,
wearing a crown of a garland of skulls, three-eyed, and with a smiling countenance.
One should meditate on all phenomena as the unsurpassed sound of the Dharma;
[the deity] is clothed in a tiger skin and draped with a human hide,
holding a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, with his right hand granting fearlessness.
Wearing a crown of five Buddhas and adorned with a garland of severed heads,
he stands in the midst of that Bhairava,
filling skull-cups with the five nectars of wisdom for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings.
The yoga of the deity Khaṭvāṅga, the skull-cup, the hero, and the yoginī;
with the right hand she displays the pure gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), which grants liberation from the remainder of existence.
By means of this, she removes all evil and the terrors of the wicked.
Wearing a crescent moon, peaceful, with a head marked by a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*), and adorned on the forehead with a vajra-garland and charming anklets;
he stands upright in the center of the pericarp upon a double-lotus with eight petals.
Having visualized the terrifying Kālarātrī, who is trampled upon by the foot of [the deity’s] wrathful gaze,
one should meditate on the Jñānasattva in that form, arisen from the syllable *vaṃ*. One should then clearly manifest Heruka as the mind-wheel within the heart.
The speech-wheel is to be meditated upon in the throat, while the body-wheel is at the crown of the head;
she has the appearance of blue, red, and white, possesses six arms and three faces,
is embraced by [the consort] holding a vajra and bell, and has three eyes and a distorted face.
Holding skull-cups and khaṭvāṅgas, and bearing tridents and severed heads,
they abide in the state of great bliss through union with their respective consorts;
they are produced from and arise within the syllables at the center of the four maṇḍalas.
Wearing a crown of garlands of skulls, they possess their own supreme emblems produced from themselves;
through the sequential yoga of the seats and so forth, there is the supreme commitment of the three yogas.
Likewise, there are Ḍākinī, Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, and Rūpiṇī.
One should place [the goddesses] in the positions of the lotuses with the four supreme skull-cups: Ḍākinī is yellow in color, Lāmā is born from the color of the Palāśa flower,
Khaṇḍarohā is blue, and Rūpiṇī is brilliantly red.
Holding a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, she displays the supreme gesture of fearlessness in her right hand.
At the gates are the four goddesses, beginning with Kākāsyā; they are the Ḍākinīs, blue, yellow, red, and green, possessing fierce forms.

In the corners are Yamadāḍhī and the others— Karālī, Bhīmā, and Bhīṣaṇī— who stand upon the four māras, holding skull-bowls and khaṭvāṅgas, as well as the gesture of supreme fearlessness, a hand-drum (ḍamaru), and a curved knife (karttikā).
The supreme goddesses have three eyes and loose hair, and they are clad in the directions as their garments.
They wear crowns of skull-ornaments and are adorned with the five mudrās.
[They hold] the mirror, clothing, fragrance, and nectar—this is the fourfold worship.
Through the sequence of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and by means of the application of mind, speech, and body,
there is the purification of the internal and external factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).
[These are represented by] the twenty-four letters beginning with *ka*, their heads marked by the nasal drop (*bindu*).

The mantra of all the heroes, joined with two *praṇavas* and ending with the syllable *phaṭ*, bestows the fruit of all desires. The *ḍākinī* is named *Praṇava*; [the mantra consists of] *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ* at the end.
Thus, the mantra-reality of the Ḍākinīs beginning with Pracaṇḍā bestows happiness;
for the Vajras of Body, Speech, and Mind, the secret syllables are HŪṂ ĀḤ OṂ.
On the lotus petals, the Praṇava (OṂ) is for the Ḍākinī, together with the neuter SAHAḤ.
The two syllables *hūṃ* and *oṃ*, along with *phaṭ* at the end, should be joined according to one's desire;
however, for the mantras beginning with Kākāsyā and the others, they are accompanied by the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*) both at the beginning and at the end.
One should join the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* at the end;
likewise, one should employ the syllables *śa*, *sa*, *ṣa*, *ha*, the *praṇava* (*oṃ*), as well as *hūṃ*, *haṃ*, and *vauṣaṭ* for the Yamadāḍhī mantra and others.
In the center, however, one should recollect the mantra of Buddhakapālī as follows:
Oṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aṃḥ kṣaḥ svāhā.

One should apply the armor of the earth-element, the effort, and the kavaca-mantra; therein, one should unify with the commitment (*samaya*) of the wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*) through the ritual of worship.
For the mantras at the end of the fourfold worship, one's own name is joined with the *praṇava* and the syllable *hūṃ*.
In this very manner, one should join the mandala arising from the Buddha-Kapālika;
one should sequentially apply the vajra ornaments to the limbs of all [the deities].

Through the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should recite that which arises from the Samaya-cakra, sequentially from the three wheels by means of the yoga of emanation and withdrawal within the four secret [centers] of the world. By this application of the ritual method, one should perform the recitation.
Through the practice of the four junctions (saṃdhyā), the supreme commitment (samaya) is accomplished—
the commitment of all mantras, the supreme Buddha-Kāpālika.
By means of the yoga of non-concentration, one should fashion everything indeed.
One should always maintain the samaya, which is the supreme nectar of the five gnoses;
or else, by reciting the mantra-tattva through the recitation of one's own name:
OṂ ŚRĪBUDDHAKĀPĀLI BUṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ ḌĀKINĪJĀLASAMVARA HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ.
Thus, when this supreme and beautiful yoga— the excellent knowledge of the Yoginīs—
is bestowed upon those who have fallen from their commitments (samaya),
peace and good fortune arise, and the Yoginī consecrates them.
Having bathed in the secret water externally according to the sequence of the four junctions,
and having taken up the pledges and the vows, one again entreats the Guru:
"Whether through ignorance or due to my deluded nature, I have fallen away from the pledges in vain."
"O Protector, Lord Vajradhara, you are my refuge;
O Great Compassionate One, Lord of the World, you are also my refuge.
Having made this firm resolve, accomplishment is certainly attained.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Arising of the Buddha-Kapāla through the Restoration of the Samaya," in the *Abhidhānottarottara*.
